claims.text: Dynamic passivation kinetics dominates the coupled wear-corrosion response in high-entropy alloys.
Sliding abrasion repeatedly disrupts the protective passive film.
Passive film disruption exposes fresh alloy surfaces to accelerated corrosion.
Total tribocorrosion degradation depends on how rapidly and effectively the passive film reforms.
An AlCrTiZrMo or CoCrFeNi-based alloy in a homogenized or annealed state can begin testing with an intact passive film in the selected electrolyte.
The governing structural mediator is continuous disruption and reformation of the passive film at the sliding interface.
More frequent film disruption or slower film regrowth increases wear-corrosion synergy.
Newly exposed active metal sites corrode faster than passivated sites.
Corrosion products can alter frictional contact, increase mechanical wear, and impede stable passivation.
Rapid film reformation will produce lower total degradation than a baseline alloy with slower passivation kinetics.
Rapid film reformation will lower both the wear and corrosion components of degradation.
Slow or mechanically fragile passive films will cause total material loss to exceed the additive sum of separately measured wear and corrosion losses.
Testing the same alloy under corrosion without sliding and wear in an inert environment eliminates or markedly reduces synergy.
Low load, low environmental aggressiveness, or extremely rapid film formation produces minimal synergy.
Under extreme load or highly corrosive conditions, ineffective film protection causes synergy to dominate and total degradation to become high.
Composition or microstructure may alter film formation, stability, or mechanical properties enough that passivation kinetics is not the sole driver.
Annealing or doping can be used to create a same-alloy variant with enhanced passivation kinetics or a denser protective oxide.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines the comparator as an alloy with slower passivation kinetics, whereas the baseline field defines the comparison as the same alloy under separate corrosion-only and inert wear-only conditions. These are different controls and do not provide one consistent matched baseline.
